content: The guidelines for HIV treatment and care are based on a public health approach that prioritizes feasibility and effectiveness across diverse settings, consistent with previous WHO recommendations. All external contributors, including members of the Guideline Development Group and the External Review Group, completed WHO declarations of interest forms in line with WHO policies. These declarations were reviewed by the WHO Guideline Steering Group, and management plans were developed and presented during the guidelines meeting. Systematic reviews and evidence-to-decision-making tables were prepared using the GRADE process and shared in advance of the meetings. Discussions were facilitated by a methodologist. The updated recommendations were finalized during a virtual meeting held from October 5–9, 2020, with all decisions made by consensus. Draft guidelines were circulated for review in November 2020. In the early stages of HIV treatment scale-up, a one-size-fits-all, clinic-based model was used, which did not account for individual needs. As national guidelines evolved to recommend antiretroviral therapy (ART) for all people living with HIV, differentiated service delivery (DSD) became essential to address the diverse needs of individuals. DSD, a person-centered approach, simplifies and adapts HIV services to meet the needs of people living with or vulnerable to HIV while optimizing health system resources. This approach applies to prevention, testing, linkage to care, ART initiation and follow-up, and integration of HIV care with management of coinfections and comorbidities. The 2016 WHO guidelines identified four groups with specific clinical needs: individuals with advanced HIV disease, those clinically well, those established on ART, and those on failing ART regimens. DSD models have primarily focused on clinically stable individuals but have expanded to address the needs of those with advanced disease, high viral loads, and comorbidities. These models also aim to improve HIV testing and prevention uptake. DSD models should consider specific populations, such as children, adolescents, pregnant and breastfeeding women, and key populations, as well as contextual factors like low HIV prevalence or emergency settings. The approach involves four building blocks: when, where, what, and who provides services. For example, clinical consultations, ART refills, and psychosocial support may be delivered separately or together, depending on the model. Since 2016, many countries, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa, have adopted DSD as part of national policy. The definition of being established on ART applies to all populations, including those on secondor third-line regimens, those with controlled comorbidities, and vulnerable groups. These populations often face challenges with retention and viral suppression, making them suitable for tailored DSD models. Group models managed by healthcare workers, such as ART adherence clubs, have shown high retention and viral suppression rates. For example, a South African study reported 95% retention at 12 months and 89% at 24 months, with 97% viral suppression. These models are cost-effective, acceptable to both clients and healthcare workers, and protective against disengagement from care. Client-managed group models, where members take turns collecting ART for the group, have also demonstrated improved retention and reduced costs. These models are particularly beneficial in decongesting clinics and supporting adherence in family groups, key populations, and unstable settings. Individual models based at facilities, such as fast-track ART refills, reduce waiting times, missed appointments, and costs while maintaining high retention and viral suppression rates. Community-based individual models, including fixed community points, mobile outreach, and home delivery, have shown high retention rates and cost-effectiveness in various settings. People-centered care is a cornerstone of effective HIV treatment. Health systems should invest in practices that improve relationships between patients and providers, such as ongoing training, mentoring, and supportive supervision. Addressing stigma and discrimination in healthcare settings is critical, particularly for key populations. Interventions to improve client-provider relationships include providing welcoming services, conducting sensitivity training, offering individualized adherence counseling, and facilitating client education. ART initiation outside health facilities is recommended as an additional option to routine facility-based initiation. Community-based HIV testing and rapid ART initiation can reduce delays and losses to care. This approach is particularly relevant for vulnerable populations who face barriers such as stigma and discrimination. Overall, differentiated service delivery models and people-centered care practices aim to improve ART uptake, adherence, and viral suppression while addressing the diverse needs of people living with HIV. These approaches are supported by evidence demonstrating their effectiveness in improving health outcomes and optimizing resources.
